stage.byline: By Michelle Pera-McGhee and David Mora

text.value: In 2009, the Australian comedy group “Axis of Awesome” performed a viral sketch showing that a surprising number of pop songs – from Journey’s “Don’t Stop Believing” to Beyoncé’s “If I Were A Boy” – are built off of the same 4 chords.
Chords provide the harmonic foundation for a song, so people cite this video as proof that all pop music is formulaic and sounds the same. The sheer volume of songs makes a compelling case.
But is it true?
Is pop music really:

li: built on a single four-chord progression 🧱

text.value: To find out, we gathered every Billboard top-20 hit since 1958, [7,300] songs, and scraped their chord progressions from popular online chord sites.
But to compare thousands of songs, we first need a way to tell when two of them are doing the same thing.
A chord is a combination of two or more notes. A chord progression is a series of chords that often loops multiple times in a song.
But the literal chord names you might be familiar with – like C, D, Ab – miss something important.

“All Too Well” goes <button>C-G-Am-F.</button> “With Or Without You” goes <button>D-A-Bm-G.</button> “Demons” goes <button>Eb-Bb-Cm-Ab.</button> On paper, these are different progressions. But to your ear, they move in the same way.
Every song has a key, a home base chord that it keeps returning to. If we name each chord instead by its distance from home, we can see that these songs actually share a chord progression.
Musicians notate this with roman numerals. The I is the home base chord, ii is a step away, iii is another step away, IV, V, vi, vii.
So, these songs all go I-V-vi-IV, which is the Axis of Awesome “four chords” progression.
Songs also differ in how much they lean on a progression. Some are 100% one progression on repeat. Others use it as one ingredient in a more varied harmonic recipe.
With those two ideas, which progressions a song uses and how much, we can put every song on the same map.
Here is every Billboard top-20 hit since 1958, arranged by the mix of progressions each one uses.

Here's how the map works. Zoom in on these islands, and you’ll see each dot as a song, placed near songs that use a similar mix of chord progressions. When enough similar songs gather in one area, they form a cluster. Songs in grey don't have enough close neighbors to belong to any cluster; their mix of progressions is too unusual.
The purists, built mostly from one progression, are at the center of each cluster, and mixed songs spread out between them.
Learn more about how we matched chord progressions and made the map in the methods.
Here is the Axis of Awesome cluster.
They were onto something, lots of songs rely heavily on this progression, but this only makes up about [2%] of songs in the dataset.
So, what’s on the rest of the map? These are the most common chord progressions in our dataset.
Let’s take a closer look at this list, because these don’t all feel the same.
Tk one of the top ones like I-IV vamp or happy walkup (maybe one for each), show examples
You’ll notice a lot of these top progressions exclusively involve I, IV, and V. If you’re gonna learn 3 chords, learn those.

text.value: There’s a reason. These are the 3 core building blocks of Western harmony that create a journey of tension and release. This goes way back, like Bach back.
The I is our home base, the starting chord of the key. It feels stable and resolved.
The IV is a little step away from home.
The V is further, more unstable. It really wants to go back to I.
Like in You’re Still The One by Shania Twain, where it ends on the V. My ear, at least, is begging for it to end back on the I and come home .
Tk doo wop?
This progression looks different than the others because it’s in a minor key.
Sometimes people say that major is happy and minor is sad, but tell that to Poker Face by Lady Gaga… Just because a song is in a minor key doesn’t mean it’s sad, it’s much more nuanced.
Instead, musicians often refer to minor as a darker sound, and major as a brighter sound. It’s like a different color palette to work with.
So pop doesn't run on just one formula. It has many, and they produce different emotional journeys.
Explore all the clusters at the end in explore mode.
Ok, but even if pop songs pull from a variety of progressions, perhaps each song just endlessly loops that single progression, without creativity or nuance?
If we want to count the number of progressions in a song, we should weight them by how often they appear.
We’ll call that a song’s number of effective progressions. That way, a song dominated by 1 progression with a 2nd that appears only once gets a score of 1.1 effective progressions, rather than 2.
There’s a pretty even split between songs with few progressions and songs with a lot of progressions.
But that has changed over time.
The median song went from 4.4 effective progressions in the 1970s (the most diverse decade) to 1.9 in the 2010s (the most homogenous).
So even though it’s not the case that most songs are just 1 loop, songs are getting loopier. The Axis of Awesome boys had their finger on something real.
What about the final claim, that progressions are deployed ubiquitously across time?
Many of the most common progressions are. There are only a few standouts that really define an era.
The Axis of Awesome sketch and its claims are a product of their time period.
“The four chords” surged in the late 2000s, their performance was in 2009. This progression is [3x] more common in the 2000s vs other decades, and was found in a full [11%] of songs.
It begs the question: Did every decade have its own version of the Axis of Awesome chord progression?
Interestingly, not really…
…with one huge exception: the 50s and 60s was dominated by doo wop.
[1 in 9] songs during that period included a doo wop progression. It was [2.6x] more common then than overall in the dataset.
The doo wop progression is I-vi-IV-V.
It’s the same 4 chords as Axis of Awesome (I-V-vi-IV), in a different order.
These two classic progressions dominated and defined their respective eras.
